## Social class

### The Relevance of Social Class

Despite criticism of class analysis [@pakulski_death_1997], contemporary studies show that class inequalities remain relevant for explaining attitudes towards inequality [@dodson_economic_2017; @lindh_public_2015; @lindh_class_2020; @kulin_class_2013]. Different approaches in class analysis agree that socioeconomic positions determine how material interests and shared experiences structure subjective perceptions of social reality and justification of inequalities [@langsaether_more_2020; @bottero_class_2004; @svallfors_moral_2006].

Class theory in welfare states suggests that labour market positions define similarities in economic resources, opportunities and constraints, structuring both economic interests and group identities [@erikson_constant_1992; @korpi_new_2003]. Market-based distribution processes mainly favor class categories with scarce productive resources, while those with fewer marketable resources benefit more from political distribution based on social citizenship [@korpi_democratic_2018; @korpi_power_2006].

### Class, Material Interests and Attitudes Toward Justice

Material interests from class position bridge objective inequality structure, justice perceptions, political positioning, and resource distribution [@bottero_class_2004; @kulin_class_2013; @langsaether_more_2020]. Studies recognize that individuals' class position—subordinate or privileged—produces significant variations in how they perceive and justify social inequalities within market frameworks [@langsaether_more_2020; @svallfors_moral_2006]. From a rational actor perspective, those with greater marketable assets favor market distribution more than those with fewer assets and greater risks [@lindh_public_2015]. In social services, private financing imposes higher individual costs and links access to income, potentially restricting access for low-income or high-risk groups [@gingrich_making_2011].

Empirical research shows fairness perceptions are structured by social position [@edlund_democratic_2015; @perezahumada_class_2024]. Lower classes tend to reject inequality and favor redistribution, while upper classes accept inequalities based on meritocratic criteria [@castillo_perceptions_2025; @lindh_public_2015; @lindh_class_2020]. This reflects that privileged individuals experience less material constraint, attribute their situation to effort and qualifications [@lindh_class_2020], and justify service access as fair market competition based on ability to pay [@castillo_perceptions_2025].

### Social Class and Market Justice 

In individual contribution systems like Chile's, class position directly determines contribution capacities and benefit outcomes. Privileged classes, with stable incomes and formal employment, maintain sustained contributions producing robust accounts and higher pensions [@gil-hernandez_wealth_2025]. Conversely, working classes face precarious trajectories with unemployment and lower wages, resulting in fragmented contributions and lower savings. These capacity differences translate directly into pension inequalities that reproduce and amplify working-life disparities into old age [@arrizabalomontoro_debate_2019; @cabib_avoiding_2025].

Regarding material interests, privileged classes have rational incentives to favor market-based pension systems, maximizing individual contributory benefits through higher contributions, larger balances, and superior pensions. For working classes, market-based pension systems are materially disadvantageous, as limited contributory capacity produces insufficient pensions, reinforcing material interest as explanation for class differences in justifying pension inequalities.

Chile's individual capitalisation system has generated enormous disparities and elderly vulnerability [@bril-mascarenhas_how_2019; @evans_assessing_2024; @cabib_avoiding_2025; @subsecretariadeprevisionsocial_percepcion_2023; @borzutzky_chiles_2016]. Despite documented discontent, recent studies show significant population willingness to justify pension inequalities based on meritocratic beliefs and market justice notions [@castillo_perceptions_2025]. This contradiction suggests distribution beliefs don't necessarily align with objective material class interests, raising questions about how social class and meritocratic beliefs interact in justifying inequalities [@busemeyer_welfare_2020; @otero_power_2024].

### The Moderating Role of Meritocratic Beliefs

Policy feedback theories emphasize that social institutions structure both economic incentives and normative frames [@pierson_when_1993; @rothstein_just_1998; @svallfors_political_2007], suggesting class conflict and market beliefs are shaped by citizens' institutional context [@svallfors_moral_2006]. Understanding how meritocratic beliefs and social position relate to justifying pension inequalities is fundamental for comprehending both discontent persistence and acceptance of unequal systems [@svallfors_moral_2006; @busemeyer_welfare_2020; @iturra-sanhueza_classbased_2025]. Welfare institutions structure material incentives and normative frameworks for evaluating policy performance [@kerner_pension_2020; @pierson_when_1993]. In individually funded systems, investment returns serve as performance signals influencing effectiveness judgments [@kerner_pension_2020], indicating attitudes form from both class interests and perceived system performance.

Meritocratic beliefs can moderate class effects on justifying inequalities. For privileged classes, high meritocracy reinforces market justification as legitimate reward for effort. For working classes, meritocratic beliefs may tension with material interests, potentially leading them to justify disadvantageous systems by internalizing individual responsibility for insufficient pensions. Analyzing these associations over time identifies how justifications evolve and factors explaining why groups maintain or modify fairness assessments.
